prompt.1: What should the government do about child care and schools?
prompt.2: What should the province do about child care and public schools?
prompt.3: What should the province's priorities be for child care and for schools from kindergarten to Grade 12?
prompt.4: Which direction should the province take on child care and on schools from kindergarten to Grade 12?
prompt.5: Choose the priority for ChildCareBC, the province's child care program, and for kindergarten to Grade 12 (K-12) schools.

context.1: Child care costs families a lot. The province pays for some low-cost spots, but it has paused adding new ones to save money. Some parties want many more low-cost spots or free child care. Others want schools to focus on reading, math and testing.
context.2: Child care can cost families as much as rent. About one in ten licensed spaces costs $10 a day, and the province has paused new $10-a-day spaces for three years to save money. Some fast-growing school districts still rely on portable classrooms. Parties disagree on whether to expand child care, focus schools on basics, or hold spending.
context.3: About 10% of licensed child care spaces cost $10 a day. In 2026 the NDP government paused new $10-a-day spaces for three years. Some fast-growing school districts still use many portable classrooms. The Greens want free child care by 2031 and CentreBC wants 20,000 more $10-a-day spaces. The Conservatives and OneBC focus on testing, grades and the basics.
context.4: About 10% of licensed child care spaces cost $10 a day. In February 2026 the NDP government paused new $10-a-day enrolment for three years to fix the program's funding model. The Affordable Child Care Benefit still helps families with incomes up to $111,000. Fast-growing school districts still use portable classrooms.
context.5: New $10-a-day enrolment has been frozen since February 2026 (reported as a three-year freeze), and Budget 2026 adds $330 million over three years for child care. There were more than 16,000 such spaces in March 2025, against a target of 20,000. The Affordable Child Care Benefit continues for family incomes up to $111,000. Budget 2026 plans $3.9 billion over three years to build, renovate and seismically upgrade schools. The Greens' October 13 platform costs child care at $260 million a year, not counting capital for new centres, and education at $587 million a year. CentreBC puts its education plan at about $2.0 billion plus $750 million in capital over four years, and funds child care from federal money, by the party's own figures.

text.2: Bring in province-wide tests in reading, writing and math, pass a parents' rights law, and don't expand child care.

text.5: Bring in standardized provincial testing focused on reading, writing and mathematics, a Parental Bill of Rights guaranteeing informed consent and classroom transparency, and no expansion of ChildCareBC.

text.2: Focus on reading and math, bring back letter grades and provincial exams, and don't expand child care.

text.5: Focus on literacy and numeracy, restore letter grades in Grades 4 to 9 and provincial exams in Grades 10 and 12, raise no new taxes, and make no child care commitment.

text.3: Add 20,000 $10-a-day spaces and 25,000 school seats, bring in letter grades for Grades 4 to 9, and fund a counsellor per 400 students.

text.1: This party made child care cheaper, then paused new low-cost spots. It has built schools, but some students still learn in portable classrooms.
text.3: The NDP created $10-a-day child care, then in 2026 froze new spaces for three years. It says it has built 250 schools, but some fast-growing districts still rely on portable classrooms. It made no new education or child care promise in 2026.
text.5: The NDP launched ChildCareBC in 2018 and had more than 16,000 $10-a-day spaces by March 2025, toward a goal of 20,000. In February 2026 it paused new enrolment and expansion, a freeze Global News reported as three years, and Budget 2026 adds $330 million over three years for child care. The party says it built 250 schools. Budget 2026 plans $3.9 billion over three years for school building and seismic upgrades. It made no education or child care commitment in 2026.

text.1: This party wants to remove a school resource on gender identity and, in 2024, promised letter grades and exams. It has made no child care promises.
text.3: The Conservatives' 2026 Safe Schools page calls for repealing SOGI 123, with no child care or school building promise. They promised letter grades and provincial exams in 2024 but have not repeated that. Their pledge of no new taxes limits new spending.
text.5: The 2026 Safe Schools page would repeal SOGI 123, a teaching resource on sexual orientation and gender identity. It has no child care, school building or post-secondary commitment. The 2024 platform promised letter grades in Grades 4 to 9 and provincial exams in Grades 10 and 12. The no-new-taxes pledge suggests school capital would be held or cut. This quiz scores the party as focused on grades and exams, with low confidence on child care.

text.1: This party wants free child care for all, better pay for child care workers, and food for every student.
text.3: The Greens would lift the freeze now, make child care free for all by 2031, pay early childhood educators $35 to $45 an hour and feed every student. Their platform costs child care at $260 million a year and education at $587 million a year.
text.5: On September 28, 2026, the Greens promised to lift the freeze 'immediately', make child care free for all by 2031 and pay early childhood educators $35 to $45 an hour by 2028. Their October 13 platform adds one point of registration for $10-a-day spaces, new spaces and priority registration for public, non-profit and Indigenous-led centres, closing the inclusive education funding gap, universal school food, a school supplies program, moving private school funding into public schools in phases and a moratorium on artificial intelligence in classrooms. Their Education Policy Brief adds a counsellor per 250 students. The platform costs child care at $260 million a year, not counting capital for new centres, and education at $587 million a year, and pays for its plans mainly with a tax on net wealth above $50 million.

text.1: This party wants many more low-cost child care spots, new classrooms, letter grades and more school counsellors.
text.3: CentreBC's October 10 platform adds 20,000 $10-a-day spaces by 2030 with federal money and 25,000 school seats by 2031, starting where portables are most common. It keeps class-size limits, funds a counsellor per 400 students and 1,500 more education assistants, and brings back letter grades. The party puts the cost at about $2 billion plus $750 million in capital.
text.5: The platform adds 20,000 $10-a-day spaces by 2030, with federal funds 'secured to 2031', and 25,000 school seats by 2031 using prefab additions and $750 million in capital. It keeps and funds class-size limits, moves to a counsellor per 400 students by 2030, adds 1,500 education assistants, brings in letter grades for Grades 4 to 9 from September 2028, publishes test results by school, caps tuition increases at 2% and sets a school artificial intelligence standard in 2027. Education costs about $2.0 billion over four years (party figure).

text.1: This party wants student testing, more say for parents, and no new child care spending.
text.3: OneBC would bring in standardized testing in reading, writing and math and a Parental Bill of Rights, and would remove SOGI 123, a teaching resource on sexual orientation and gender identity. It has no child care plan.
text.5: OneBC's priorities are standardized testing focused on reading, writing and mathematics, a Parental Bill of Rights, and removing SOGI 123 (a sexual orientation and gender identity resource) and 'politicized content' from classrooms. It has no child care, school building or post-secondary commitments, and its 25% tax cuts and four-year plan to balance the budget limit new spending.

scoring_rationale: Five options. a = OneBC (4): standardized testing, Parental Bill of Rights, no child care spending; Conservative 3 (shares the testing focus and no child care pledge, has not proposed a Parental Bill of Rights in 2026). A teacher strike ban was removed from option a on October 13 because no party or news source for it was found; CentreBC 1 (published FSA results by school, nothing else). b = Conservative (4): basics-first with the 2024 letter-grade and exam pledges and no child care commitment inside a no-new-taxes frame; OneBC 3; CentreBC 2 (the same letter grades Grades 4-9 and literacy and numeracy focus, but the opposite on child care); NDP 1 (its freeze matches the no-expansion element, nothing else). c = NDP record (4): it built $10-a-day and then froze it, so the freeze is the operative position regardless of 2024 rhetoric; Conservative 2 (no expansion fits its fiscal frame, but it would not defend the program); CentreBC 1 (would lift the freeze, keeps building); OneBC 1. d = CentreBC's platform (4): 20,000 spaces, 25,000 seats, counsellors, letter grades; Green 3 (goes further on child care, shares counsellors and food, differs on grades and AI); NDP 2 (created $10-a-day and builds seats, now paused); Conservative 1 (letter grades only; a symmetry fix from 0 now that the option carries a grading element); OneBC 0. e = Green (4); CentreBC 2 (expands spaces and school food, not free care or an ECE wage grid); NDP 1 (same goal in 2018, opposite action in 2026). SOGI 123 is scored only in its own question. Symmetry: Conservative on a (3) and OneBC on b (3); Conservative on d (1) and CentreBC on b (2).
